paragraphs.title: The Symbol of the Hair and the Division of Fate

answers: A sharp knife and a barber's razor
A trumpet and a lamp
A shield and a spear
easy.explanation: He was told to take a sharp knife and a barber's razor.
easy.q: What was the prophet commanded to take at the beginning of the passage?

answers: Two parts
Three parts
Five parts
easy.explanation: The hair was divided into three parts.
easy.q: Into how many parts was the hair divided?

answers: It was buried in the ground
It was thrown into the water
It was burned in the midst of the city
easy.explanation: One third was burned with fire in the midst of the city.
easy.q: What was done with one third of the hair?

answers: Different forms of judgment and destruction
Three kings
Three temples
medium.explanation: The portions picture burning, being struck with the sword, and scattering.
medium.q: What do the three portions of hair represent in the passage?

answers: It was placed in a vessel
A sword was drawn out after it
It was returned to the city
medium.explanation: The LORD said that He would draw out a sword after the scattered portion.
medium.q: What happened to the third that was scattered in the wind?

answers: A small number of hairs taken from the remainder
A large number of soldiers
A few days of siege
medium.explanation: A small remnant of the hairs was bound in the prophet’s garment.
medium.q: What does “a few in number” mean in this passage?

answers: The remnant is guaranteed to escape
Danger continues even after the first escape
The fire has no connection with the people’s fate
challenge.explanation: Even part of the small remnant is taken and burned.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the fact that some of the small remnant is cast into the fire again?

answers: Division, shaving, scattering, burning
Shaving, division, treatment of the thirds, taking a remnant
Burning, taking a remnant, shaving, division
challenge.explanation: The hair is shaved, divided, dealt with in portions, and a remnant is taken.
challenge.q: Which order correctly describes the prophet’s actions?

answers: It will go forth into all the house of Israel
It will light the temple
It will put out the sword
challenge.explanation: The passage says that a fire will come forth from it into all Israel.
challenge.q: What is the significance of the fire that comes forth from the remnant?

paragraphs.title: Jerusalem among the Nations and Its Guilt

answers: In the midst of the nations and countries
Outside every country
Only in the wilderness
easy.explanation: The LORD said He had set Jerusalem in the midst of the nations.

answers: She kept them perfectly
She changed them into wickedness
She taught them to the nations
easy.explanation: Jerusalem changed the LORD’s judgments into wickedness.
easy.q: What did Jerusalem do to God’s judgments?

answers: In the sight of the nations
Before the priests only
Before the king only
easy.explanation: The judgments would be executed in Jerusalem in the sight of the nations.
easy.q: Before whom would the judgments be executed?

answers: She did not walk in God’s statutes or keep His judgments
She was far away from the nations
She had no countries around her
medium.explanation: Her guilt included refusing God’s judgments and statutes.
medium.q: Why was Jerusalem judged according to the passage?

answers: Detestable and wicked acts
Good laws
Songs of joy
medium.explanation: “Abominations” refers to acts that are detestable and deeply offensive.
medium.q: What does the KJV word “abominations” mean in this context?

answers: Her actions are presented as the reason for the judgment
Her actions cancel the judgments
There is no connection between them
medium.explanation: The judgments come because she rejected God’s ways and committed abominations.
medium.q: What is the relationship between Jerusalem’s actions and the judgments against her?

answers: She did not even act according to the judgments of the nations around her
She was smaller than the surrounding countries
She was not surrounded by other nations
challenge.explanation: The passage says she did not even do according to the judgments of the nations around her.
challenge.q: What was especially serious about Jerusalem’s behavior?

answers: Her responsibility and public exposure before the nations
Her complete isolation from outside influence
Her lack of connection with surrounding countries
challenge.explanation: Her central position highlights both her responsibility and the public nature of her judgment.
challenge.q: What is emphasized by presenting Jerusalem in the midst of the nations?

answers: The guilt involved both rejecting laws and failing to practice justice
The people were commanded only to build a city
The laws had no connection with the punishment
challenge.explanation: The passage stresses both refusal to keep God’s statutes and failure to do His judgments.
challenge.q: What does the repeated mention of judgments and statutes emphasize?

paragraphs.title: Famine, Defilement of the Sanctuary, and the Division of Punishment

answers: The sanctuary
The rivers
The gates only
easy.explanation: They had defiled the LORD’s sanctuary with detestable things and abominations.

answers: By pestilence, famine, the sword, and scattering
By peace, rain, and blessing
By building, trade, and celebration
easy.explanation: The passage describes pestilence, famine, death by the sword, and scattering.
easy.q: How was the punishment divided among the people?

answers: That the LORD had spoken and acted
That the nations had acted alone
That the famine had never happened
easy.explanation: They would know that the LORD had spoken and carried out His judgment.
easy.q: What would the people know after the LORD’s anger was accomplished?

answers: The defilement is given as a reason the LORD would not spare them
The defilement cancels the punishment
They are unrelated
medium.explanation: Their defilement is stated before the declaration of judgment.
medium.q: How are the defilement of the sanctuary and the punishment connected?

answers: The source and support of food
A staff used in battle
A pillar in the sanctuary
medium.explanation: Breaking the staff of bread pictures the removal of food and sustenance.
medium.q: What does the expression “staff of bread” mean in the passage?

answers: Pestilence and famine, the sword, and scattering into the winds
The sword, scattering, and pestilence and famine
Scattering, famine, and the sword
medium.explanation: One third dies by pestilence and famine, one falls by the sword, and one is scattered.
medium.q: What is the correct order of the three portions in the passage?

answers: That the punishment would come in several different forms
That everyone would escape in the same way
That the punishment concerned only the sanctuary
challenge.explanation: Each third suffers a different form of judgment.
challenge.q: What does the division of the people into thirds emphasize?

answers: It identifies the LORD as the one who carried out the judgment
It cancels all the punishment
It describes the beginning of the siege
challenge.explanation: The statement points to recognition of the LORD after the judgment is completed.
challenge.q: What is the purpose of the statement, “they shall know that I the LORD have spoken it”?

answers: The judgment will be carried out without pity
The people will receive abundant food
The sanctuary will immediately be rebuilt
challenge.explanation: The expression emphasizes that the LORD will not spare or pity them in the judgment.
challenge.q: What is conveyed by the words “neither shall mine eye spare”?

paragraphs.title: Jerusalem’s Disgrace and the Arrows of Famine

answers: A waste and a reproach
A place of joy
A fruitful land
easy.explanation: The LORD said He would make Jerusalem waste and a reproach.

answers: Famine sent against the people for their destruction
Musical instruments in the sanctuary
Heavy rains
easy.explanation: The arrows are a picture of the destructive famine sent upon them.
easy.q: What do the “evil arrows of famine” represent?

answers: Famine, evil beasts, pestilence, blood, and the sword
Rain, peace, blessing, and rest
Trade, building, and celebration
easy.explanation: The final verse names famine, evil beasts, pestilence, blood, and the sword.
easy.q: Which afflictions are mentioned at the end of the passage?

answers: Through the waste, reproach, and judgments brought upon her
Through her wealth
Through the peace within her
medium.explanation: The surrounding nations would see her disgrace and the judgments executed in her.
medium.q: How would Jerusalem become an example among the nations?

answers: Desolate and ruined
Full of abundance
Protected and secure
medium.explanation: Here “waste” describes a condition of desolation and ruin.
medium.q: What does the KJV word “waste” mean in this passage?

answers: Breaking the source of bread leads to scarcity and famine
Breaking the bread brings abundance
The two descriptions are unrelated
medium.explanation: The broken staff of bread represents the loss of food supplies.
medium.q: What is the connection between breaking the staff of bread and the famine?

answers: To show that the destruction will be visible to everyone
To hide Jerusalem’s condition
To describe her rebuilding
challenge.explanation: Her reproach will be seen by all who pass by.
challenge.q: Why are those who pass by described as witnesses to Jerusalem’s disgrace?

answers: The people will face several different dangers, not famine alone
Famine is only a figure and will affect no one
The sword is not mentioned at all
challenge.explanation: In addition to famine, the passage lists beasts, pestilence, blood, and the sword.
challenge.q: What does the variety of afflictions reveal about the severity of the judgment?

answers: Her condition will serve as a warning and example to surrounding nations
She will teach the nations how to celebrate
She will become a center of commerce
challenge.explanation: Her judgment will instruct the nations by showing the consequences of her wickedness.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between Jerusalem’s reproach and her being an instruction to the nations?
